chapter: Averty's letters and Tom Brown's claims
title: La Rocca answers Brown's claims and describes his campaign
summary: La Rocca disputes Brown's name changes, band personnel and Lamb's, and says he now works on this in semi-retirement with a photostat machine.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, he wrote down to Mr. Howard Jacobs. He put a piece in the paper for asking for an old time jazz band to write him. That he was trying to clear up the great mystery that hangs over the jazz. That someone should get credit where it should be. Now many people ask, amongst this one was this Tom Brown and the record changer. Well, now these things I had never known before, the record changer, the claims that Brown made. These had just come to my mind. Now when you have a family to support you, just don't jump up and go here and run, I am a lawyer, when you have business to make a living for your family. I let that slide along a little bit. I kept corresponding with the man to see if I could get some more out of him. If you notice, Brown says that his name was Brown's band from Dixieland. Brown's Ragtime Band. Then later he changed to Five Ragtime Roots. Then he was Five Kings of Ragtimes. Then he taken the name of the original Dixieland Jazz Band. He had the first one. He says, I admit to him, on a television program, this is a lie. When he seen me there, he started to run away. I said, Tom, you don't have to be afraid of me. Go out and tell what you did. You're entitled to have your place in this world. I said, you did go before us, but I didn't say he was a Dixieland Jazz Band and I didn't say he played like us. Because he had many other musicians that went before him. All the more that they went, none of them was recognized. It was the original Dixieland Jazz Band that was recognized for that type of music. None of them made a success. I don't care how many went. That didn't mean anything. Then he goes on to further say that they stood several years. Now from May to October is not a year. And in November, Shields was playing with me again. He had played with me in New Orleans before he left there. The original band, Brown's band consisted of Gussie Miller, clarinet, lamb and drums, light piano guitar, Steve Brown bass, Tom Brown trombone, and Ray Lopez carnit. That was the original band. And after they went up there, they met a fellow named Byrd Kelly. Byrd Kelly asked him if they could get a clarinet player from him. That he wanted to put one in his band. They sent down for Lawrence Shields. Shields was brought up there. Shields didn't like the type of music that was playing. It was going to come to New Orleans. Then the swap was made. He said Shields played with him several years. That man's lying. He said he went through one big contract at Lamb's Cafe and had signed another one for a longer time. How could he sign anonymous for a longer time when he said the place was closed for repairs? There is no place that the original Dixieland Jazz ever played that was closed for repairs. They remodeled while we were playing there and they lodged them, but they never closed them for repairs. So this man was no success. But with the help of a jazz band who give him loving cups. And men who are supposed to be prophets, that they was to discredit me and give the Negro credit. All their publications carried his story. This being a young man in France, it was hard for him to believe what he reads is right. So he contacted me. And I'll have a bunch of letters that I have in the files will be in there. And you jazz scholars want to look them up. You can see how these people treat this jazz business. Starting with Marshall Stein, who I say has got to be pro-communist. He is not anything else but that. Because no man writes untruth about a man and knowingly prints it. Then he came to New Orleans and they did the same thing with the aid of other people here. Now this man has lied all along. I had this man just recently in 1957. I went down to my lawyers. I'm partly retired now. You know when you get 65 years of age, you get social security. All the $13,000 or $1,500 a year I got from the government for my kids, which are all miners and myself, that made me work a little easier and devote more time to clean up this jazz situation. The first thing I did was to go buy a photostatic machine. And whenever anything appeared in anywhere in the paper, I bombarded them. They may have thrown them in the gutter. They may have thrown them in the wastebasket. But some of them must have found the right place. Because the hand of God moves slow. When I had Brown to bring him before the law, I offered to go before the jazz club. These people are entrenched. They're historians. They know everything. And I was willing to go before their tribunal and meet all comers, that is Dr. Sushant and whoever they had over there, to show what they had, to dispute me. There was no takers. He was well rehearsed. This lawyer was only trying to feint him into an opening, so he could get at these bigwigs, supposed to be men of history. History that know nothing about history. My child, five years old, knows more about history of jazz than they do. Because they weren't around. I want you to read this here from Harry Sushant, a letter that Mr. Hyman sent to him, to try to get Mr. Brown and the jazz club straightened out. Read this pen.
